evidence.k1: A tenant who knows this can avoid syncing, for example by staying out of signal
evidence.k2: A thief or dishonest tenant can stop the app from uploading, or can use a modified app
evidence.k3: One manager opens the unit alone and photographs the contents. This is a classic insider risk
evidence.k4: an attacker is not trying to hit one tenant, any tenant will do

evidence.k1: The revoked person can block their own revocation.
evidence.k2: Someone who wants no trace can simply never upload.
evidence.k3: If the tenant later says items are missing, your only record is the manager's.
evidence.k4: roughly 1 guess in 900 hits a real tenant

evidence.k1: An attacker who knows they are being removed can simply stay out of sync.
evidence.k2: The record comes from the phone, which the tenant controls.
evidence.k3: Any manager can generate a code for any unit... That is an insider-theft path
evidence.k4: about 1 in 900 random guesses hits a valid PIN

evidence.k1: The attacker is often the one holding the app.
evidence.k2: The history is therefore produced and delivered by the person being logged.
evidence.k3: One person with sole access can remove items before taking the photos.
evidence.k4: 1,100 of the 1,000,000 possible 6-digit PINs are valid.
